paras: The Indianola post office affair was a dispute in Indianola, Sunflower County, Mississippi, in which white citizens pressed Minnie M. Cox, the town's Black postmistress, to resign in late 1902, and the federal government closed the office rather than accept her resignation. President Roosevelt's administration said the resignation had been forced by threats from "a brutal and lawless element," while Cox, her husband and white townspeople denied that she had been threatened. The case was debated in the Senate and credited with aiding James K. Vardaman's campaign for governor; the office reopened in January 1904 under a white postmaster.

According to the statement issued for the President, Cox had served three years as postmaster under President Harrison, was reappointed by President McKinley in 1897, and owned with her husband $10,000 to $15,000 worth of property in the county. The Cleveland Gazette added that her husband, Wayne Cox, was a railway mail clerk and that Indianola had about 700 people, more than half of them Black.

Judge S. P. Chapman, writing for the citizens, said a meeting about October 1, 1902, appointed a committee of three to circulate a petition asking Cox to resign, while a Commercial-Appeal dispatch placed the mass meeting in November. A Louisville Courier-Journal correspondent reported that the mayor chaired the meeting at the courthouse and that fifty-four citizens, "bankers, lawyers and merchants," signed the request. Chapman stated that Wayne Cox then brought him his wife's signed resignation to be read to the gathering.

The resignation took effect January 1, 1903, and the office closed. At a cabinet meeting the next day the administration refused the resignation and kept the office closed until the townspeople would accept her, sending Indianola's mail to Greenville. Its statement said the mayor and the sheriff had told a postoffice inspector they could not be answerable for her safety if she refused to resign. On January 5 or 6 Cox left for Birmingham, Alabama, saying she would not take the office again under any circumstances.

On January 24 Senator Spooner of Wisconsin defended the closing in the Senate and read letters from A. B. Weeks, a white Republican who had sought the post since October, while Senator McLaurin of Mississippi argued that the citizens had a right to petition. White residents paid a private carrier for their mail, and in April the Post Office Department said Cox's resignation had still not been accepted and she continued to draw her salary. In January 1904 the President appointed W. B. Martin, a white man who had been one of Cox's bondsmen, and the office reopened; no report of arrests or prosecutions appears in the coverage.

Northern papers carrying the administration's statement framed it as an outrage, the Minneapolis Journal heading it "Intolerable Outrage." Dispatches from Indianola instead carried the townspeople's side under heads such as "No Threats Against Woman" and "Indianola Is Indignant," quoting residents who called the closing "peanut" politics. The New Orleans Times-Democrat, reprinted in the Houston Daily Post, wrote that the situation required only that "a white citizen be appointed in place of the negro," and the Washington Times later called the forced resignation "a boon to the negro woman."

Black papers treated the case as the intimidation of a federal officer and repeatedly recalled the killing of Postmaster Baker at Lake City, South Carolina. The Los Angeles Liberator wrote that Cox resigned "to keep the white men of that town from murdering her in the streets," and the Richmond Planet blamed whites "under the influence of a white man, who was candidate for the office." The Cleveland Gazette headed its portrait of Cox "Driven From Office by Southern White Brutes" and named Mayor J. L. Davis and his brother-in-law Weeks as seeking her removal. The Colored American praised the President and reported "talk of race war."

Whether Cox was threatened remained in dispute. The administration, citing inspectors' reports and "reputable white citizens," said the resignation was "obtained under terror of threats." Cox, however, denied that violence had been threatened, and her husband said "two prominent citizens" had advised her to resign. Chapman stated that no threats were made at either meeting, and the Age-Herald noted that Spooner gave no names of those who had threatened her.

bases: White citizens of Indianola, through a mass meeting and petition, forced the Black postmistress to resign; the administration said under threats to her life, which the town and Cox denied, and no violence is reported (A5, A10, A11, A12).

That Cox resigned under a citizens' petition demanding a white postmaster is reported on all sides (A5, A10, A11), but the administration's claim that she was threatened is denied by Cox, her husband and the town's spokesmen (A10, A11, A12).

accounts.label: Administration (Cortelyou statement)
accounts.gist: Inspectors and reputable white citizens showed the resignation was forced by a lawless element on account of her color, under terror of threats; mayor and sheriff could not answer for her safety.

accounts.label: Cox and her husband
accounts.gist: She denied being threatened or subjected to indignities; her husband said two prominent citizens advised resignation and that he understood the race problem.

accounts.label: Indianola citizens (Chapman statement; Commercial-Appeal dispatch)
accounts.gist: A mass meeting petitioned for a white postmaster; Wayne Cox delivered the resignation voluntarily; no threats or intimidation were made.

accounts.label: Black editorialists
accounts.gist: Cox was driven out by threats against her life from whites who objected to her color and prosperity and wanted the post for a white man.

framing.detail: Northern papers printed the administration statement under heads like 'Intolerable Outrage' and 'Driven to Resign by a Lawless Element'.
Southern dispatches and editorials denied threats and defended a white-only post office ('No Threats Against Woman', 'Indianola Is Indignant'; Times-Democrat).
The Washington Times reported Cox drew pay without duties, calling the forced resignation 'a boon to the negro woman'.
Editorials headed 'Another Outrage', 'Intimidating a Government Official', 'Driven From Office by Southern White Brutes', linking the case to the Baker killing.

versions.value: Resignation obtained under terror of threats; her life endangered

conflicts.note: The administration cited inspectors' reports but, per the Age-Herald, Spooner could not name those who threatened her; Cox's denial was made while still in town, just before leaving.
